candidates.topic: The Baader-Meinhof Phenomenon — Why You See Things Everywhere After Learning About Them
candidates.teaser: The moment you learn a new word, it starts appearing everywhere — and science has a disturbing explanation for why.
candidates.video_description: The Baader-Meinhof Phenomenon makes your brain highlight newly learned information as if the world suddenly changed. It didn't — your perception did. Neuroscientists call it frequency illusion, and it reveals how selective your attention truly is.
candidates.script: You learn a new word, and suddenly it's everywhere — on billboards, in conversations, on TV. The world didn't change. Your brain did. It's called the Baader-Meinhof Phenomenon, and it's proof your mind filters out roughly 99% of reality at any given moment. Once something is labeled 'important,' your brain's reticular activating system flags every instance it previously ignored. You were always seeing it. You just weren't allowed to notice. So what else is your brain hiding from you right now?

candidates.topic: The Singing Sand Dunes — Desert That Produces Music
candidates.teaser: Some deserts in the world produce a deep, haunting roar — and for centuries, nobody could explain it.
candidates.video_description: Certain sand dunes around the world emit a low, resonant hum that can reach 105 decibels — louder than a motorcycle. Scientists only cracked the mystery in 2012. The answer involves sand grain size, humidity, and accidental acoustics on a massive scale.
candidates.script: Some deserts in the Sahara, Gobi, and Arabian Peninsula produce a booming roar reaching 105 decibels — louder than a motorcycle — with no storm in sight. For centuries, explorers thought they were hearing spirits. Marco Polo wrote about it in 1295. The real answer wasn't confirmed until 2012: sand grains of a very specific size, sliding in synchrony, vibrate at identical frequencies and amplify each other like a natural pipe organ. An entire desert, singing in unison. What does it sound like? Exactly like a low-flying aircraft that never arrives.

candidates.topic: The Man Who Lived Inside an Airport for 18 Years
candidates.teaser: One man checked into an airport terminal — and didn't leave for 18 years, becoming legally invisible to two governments at once.
candidates.video_title: The Man Trapped in an Airport for 18 Years
candidates.video_description: Mehran Karimi Nasseri arrived at Charles de Gaulle Airport in 1988 and legally could not leave until 2006 — a stateless man caught between bureaucracies. His case inspired the Steven Spielberg film 'The Terminal.' The real story is far stranger than the movie.
candidates.script: In 1988, a man arrived at Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport and could not leave — not for days, not for months. For 18 years. Mehran Karimi Nasseri had his refugee documents stolen, leaving him legally recognized by no country on Earth. France couldn't deport him. Iran wouldn't take him. He lived in Terminal 1, sleeping on a bench, reading newspapers, writing a diary. Airport staff brought him food. He became a local celebrity. In 2006, he finally left — and immediately collapsed from the shock of the outside world.

candidates.topic: Tardigrade — The Only Animal That Can Survive in Open Space
candidates.teaser: One creature on Earth has already survived open space — no suit, no oxygen, no protection — and came back alive.
candidates.video_title: The Animal That Survived Outer Space Naked
candidates.video_description: Tardigrades, microscopic animals under 1mm long, were exposed to the vacuum and radiation of open space in 2007 and survived. They can withstand temperatures from -272°C to 150°C, pressures six times the deepest ocean, and radiation doses lethal to every other known animal. Scientists still don't fully understand how.
candidates.script: In 2007, scientists strapped living animals to the outside of a spacecraft and launched them into open space — no suit, no oxygen, exposed to hard vacuum and full solar radiation. Ten days later, they brought them back. Most were still alive. Tardigrades, less than one millimeter long, can survive temperatures near absolute zero, pressures six times deeper than the Mariana Trench, and radiation doses 1,000 times lethal to humans. They've existed for 530 million years. If Earth ended tomorrow, they'd probably be fine. The real question is: why are they built for environments that don't exist here?

candidates.topic: The Stolen Painting That Hung in Plain Sight for 30 Years — Louvre Fake
candidates.teaser: A priceless painting hung on the wall of one of the world's most famous museums for years — and nobody realized it was a forgery.
candidates.video_title: The Louvre Hung a Fake for Years
candidates.video_description: Art forgery has fooled even the world's greatest museums, but few cases are as quietly unsettling as works that passed every expert eye for decades. The psychology of authority bias means once something is authenticated, almost no one looks again. Forgers have exploited this for centuries.
candidates.script: A painting hung inside one of the most visited museums on Earth — examined by curators, photographed by tourists, studied by scholars — and it was a fake. Art forgery doesn't just fool amateurs. It exploits a psychological flaw called authority bias: once an expert says something is real, almost no one questions it again. The most successful forgers in history didn't paint well — they painted old. Cracked varnish, aged canvas, period-accurate pigments. One forger, Han van Meegeren, sold fakes to Hermann Göring during WWII and only confessed to save himself from execution for treason. The forgery was his alibi.
